comments.author: mpyne
comments.text:
OK, I think I see what’s going on with this, in this configuration.
The goal from an attacker’s perspective is to get this to be true: `$ret = crypt($pw, $hash); $ret == $hash` when called by OpenSSH’s sshd. This is how sshd validates that the user logging in knew the account password.
The `$hash` is the “settings” to the crypt call and will normally look like “$6$--gibberish” for users with passwords set, but could look like “*” or “!” for users not intended to be able to login.
The bug is from the intersection of all of these things:
1. musl can return “*” for errors, rather than leave the return value NULL. Other libc have adopted something like this too, but seem to use a different result “*0”.
2. musl can also return “+” for errors, but only does so if $hash starts with “*”. This is intended to eliminate the possibility of an error causing `$ret == $hash` to be true, however it assumes that applications calling `crypt()` will set $pw and $hash to values corresponding to the `$ret == $hash` comparison to be made immediately afterwards.
3. OpenSSH can be convinced to pass the hash of a different user if the hash is “*” or “!” to avoid timing attacks that can enumerate the user l

The whole story is a bit worse than this.  Musl
already worked around this type of failure
.  See the second-to-last line here:
https://git.musl-libc.org/cgit/musl/tree/src/crypt/crypt_des...
(hey, this workaround is wrong if the salt is "x"!)
but they forgot to work around it here:
https://git.musl-libc.org/cgit/musl/tree/src/crypt/crypt_sha...
The vulnerable path in musl is only a little bit vulnerable, because "*" is not actually a
sha256
encrypted configuration and should not reach this code: musl's crypt(..., "*") will not call that code!  Turns out that sshd detects that the password hash is too short
and does not forward the salt
!
https://github.com/openssh/openssh-portable/blob/master/auth...
Look, no else statement!  If that if doesn't get taken, then salt remains NULL.  And the sshd code is really quite messy and doesn't keep track of the fact that this code path is inappropriate for validating an existing password hash.
A workaround in the sha256 path in musl wouldn't even have prevented the bug!
I'm going to give some credit to musl for unwisely using "*" and some credit to OpenSSH for having nonsensical control and data flow.

comments.author: aljgz
comments.text:
My general rule of thumb is: "no magic strings". This is much easier to implement in higher-level languages and when writing application/web code than system programming.
Don't return empty string/asterisk/anything else. Instead, return a failure value.
When absolutely needed, choose the magic string with more caution:
One string showing the SHA-256 of a non-existing hash? It's a good idea for it to be a valid hash. Now we have a new risk: if it's broken once, it's broken for all. So it's a good idea for it to be a random one for each machine and/or account. Even this might have problems I can't think of, but it seems to be as secure as an account with a real password.
If this is not a good decision for some reason, choose something unmistakable: "--ACCOUNT-HAS-NO-PASSWORD--". This is much less likely to be mistakenly used in a different context, is much easier to look up in a code base than "*", and is self-documenting.

comments.text:
musl’s crypt() returns the string * as an error indicator when the key is over 256 bytes long. * is also exactly what the stored field contains for every account with no password, so the “hash” matches and the login succeeds.
Does anyone know why musl does this? Are they the only C library that behaves this way?
For a C library that famously tries to adhere to POSIX as much as possible, this seems like a crazy choice. From POSIX standard:
Upon successful completion, crypt() shall return a pointer to the encoded string. The first two bytes of the returned value shall be those of the salt argument. Otherwise, it shall return a null pointer and set errno to indicate the error.
https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/functions/c...

IMO this is where languages like Rust shine. The design patterns built into the language for handling errors (Result) - force you to handle errors / function results with sentinels, null pointers, or errnos are so much more error prone than handling a Result<T,E> using a match statement.
crypt() returning `*` is insane especially since these kinds of sentinels are all over /etc/passwd

> What is it like to hear vocal folds vibrate?
I wouldn't normally describe hearing a voice as hearing "vibrations". Vibrations are indeed the physical basis of sound, and the auditory system detects changes in air pressure caused by them. But vibrations can also be perceived through touch, and the subjective experience of hearing is quite different from the tactile sensation of feeling something vibrate. When talking about feeling vibrations, I usually think of the touching sensation.
Still, both sensations originate from the same physical phenomenon. You can try to feel your own vocal chords vibrate by placing your fingers on your throat while humming. It's certainly a very different sensation, and touch generally conveys fewer acoustic details than typical hearing, but you're sensing the same underlying physical event.
One interesting example is Dani Valeska (Instagram: @daniivaleska), a Brazilian Sign Language interpreter whose husband is deaf (I couldn't find his name). - Ultimately, advertisers aren't _merely_ trying to find things you want. They're trying to get you to buy _their_ things. I 100% disagree with this. Supply chain attacks are already at an all-time high due to agentic hacking assistance, and that trend shows no sign of slowing. Every dependency you add is another potential attack vector, and just checking the dependency’s code doesn’t solve the issue - your dependencies also have dependencies!

I asked him with the first disk was, and I remember distinctly he said it was an operating system.  I asked him what an operating system was, and he said it was like a program, it was a program technically, that makes it easier to run other programs, just it was a program that didn't do much on its own and you wouldn't use it without another program right afterward.  I said it didn't seem easier if you had to load a different disk than the one you wanted to use, and you still had to load the one you wanted afterward. He looked at me disdainfully and patiently explained that all or almost all the software in the future would use operating systems and they whole process would get easier or even invisible but there would always be an operating system in there somewhere at some point in the very near future. I imagined an operating system as a dressed up software library, which was more intuitive to me as a concept.

After they announced the formalization of the classification of Finite Simple Groups, I immediately wondered "What would happen if you tried to formalize the Stacks Project?"  Despite also being very long, it's the opposite of the CFSG: instead of a poorly organized set of results that contribute to proving one big theorem, it's instead a carefully-organized set of results that cover a broad area.
The Stacks Project was the model for how mathematics should be done (at least for the pre-LLM era).  Algebraic geometry had lots of poorly organized foundational results that were not really created for themselves, but in order to solve problems in the field.  One person, Aise Johan de Jong, set out to fix it by organizing a project to write out the proofs of all of the results in a carefully organized fashion.  He's led the project since, though of course there are multiple contributors.  The whole thing is thousands of pages.
I would be interested in hearing more about the gaps they uncovered in the existing results, and how they fixed them.

stories.title_en: We can do better than line-buffered output

comments.author: Veserv
comments.text:
Yes, basically all buffering should use work-or-time based flushing.
Work-based flushing exists to batch work to amortize overhead. It allows you to tune how much time you spend in overhead in a work period. However, this can result in unbounded delay.
Time-based flushing targets a worst-case latency in low throughput environments. This ensures you do not get unbounded delays. Interestingly, this also allows you to tune how much time you spend in overhead in a work period.
So, with work-or-time based flushing what you are really tuning is how much time you are willing to spend in overhead in a work period and balancing that against latency.
As a nit, the article calls this a derivative of Nagle’s algorithm, but it is basically the opposite. Nagle’s algorithm is about batching until acknowledgement with no mention of time. In fact, the lack of time-based flushing in Nagle’s algorithm is why it interacts so poorly with TCP Delayed Ack.

comments.author: brkomir
comments.text:
I usually run 4-5 claude sessions in parallel on the same branch, each with its own working plan or work item. They coordinate almost in real time, leaving messages in a shared queue and picking them up every 30 seconds. What keeps them from stepping over each other's work is a commit script that allows only staged changes from one session to be committed at a time.
Where it actually pays off to have separate sessions is the code review. Every code change that affects how the app behaves is checked by a session that didn't write the change. Some numbers: 4,454 verdicts on 4,471 commits since September. About four in five first reviews found something, and about half asked for changes.

Brilliant! Base model releases are exactly what we need right now. This is the reliable way to do alignment. Releasing the base model then letting everyone on the planet do whatever they want with it is probably what ends up preventing extreme value drift through the intelligence explosion. Millions of people would try to align these base models in their own way, and we'll probably all fail, but those models would drift in different directions so their actions cancel eachother out in the real world. The end result is alignment to humanity's average objective function, at the civilization level. It's a messy but very surefire way to align.
There will still be a different kind of value drift from increasing intelligence itself, but that's unavoidable no matter what we do. Releasing open models slows that down too because it discourages investment in future training runs. And this strategy works unilaterally without cooperation - every open model release slows it down by a little bit. This is the actual way to pace the frontier unlike the regulatory capture stunts Anthropic and OpenAI are attempting while pontificating about their moral superiority.
